# Importance is declared config, generated by an agent

## Context

`er` needs a way to rank files by how much of the codebase depends on them, available
before any review has run. `CONTEXT.md` names this **importance**; the article that
prompted it calls the idea *blast radius*.

Every existing ranking signal is a reviewer's opinion produced during a review
(`ErFileReview.risk`, `TriageDiffStats.approx_risk`). An unreviewed diff has no
ordering at all.

The obvious implementation is a computed reverse-dependency count. It was measured
before committing.

**Cost was not the problem.** A single combined pass (`grep -rowFf patterns` over
`crates` + `desktop-ui`) takes about 30ms for 10 patterns — roughly 10× faster than
one grep per file, cheap enough to run per refresh on a worker thread.

**Accuracy was.** Run against a real changed-file set, the highest-scoring
"foundational" files came back as `mod`, `commands` and `package`. Basename-stripping
turns `mod.rs` and `commands.rs` into patterns that match every `mod` keyword in the
tree. The proxy fails precisely on module-root files — `mod.rs`, `index.ts`, `lib.rs`
— which in Rust and TypeScript are both common and the most likely to genuinely be
foundational. An earlier, encouraging measurement had used hand-picked distinctive
basenames and was measuring the easy case.

Language-aware import parsing would fix it, at the cost of a parser per language and
ongoing maintenance as the repo's languages change.

## Decision

Importance is a set of **declared rules** in the user's global config, keyed by repo:

```toml
[importance.easy-review]
"crates/er-engine/src/app/**" = "foundational"
"*.md"                        = "isolated"
```

Precedence runs most-specific-first: exact path, then glob, then file type, then a
default. The shape mirrors `PackagesConfig`
(`crates/er-engine/src/config/mod.rs:92`), which already gives `[packages.<name>]`
tables in the same file.

An agent generates those rules, using import counting as internal legwork. The count
is never surfaced to a user. What ships is a rule set a human can read, argue with,
and hand-edit.

Validation is a **distribution report** rather than a bound: the agent prints how many
files each tier captures, because the real failure mode is one glob a directory too
broad — which parses perfectly and quietly ruins the ranking.

Two tiers plus a default (`foundational`, `isolated`, `normal`). The flag-guarded
tier considered alongside them is cut: being behind a feature flag is orthogonal to
dependency weight, and it was the least reliable of the three signals.

## Consequences

**Good.** Ranking works with no review run and no model call at review time. The rules
are inspectable and correctable, which a computed score is not — "why is this file
foundational?" is answered by naming the rule that matched. No parser to maintain per
language. The generation cost is paid once per repo rather than per refresh.

**Costs.** Every repo needs a generation pass before importance does anything;
un-generated repos get the default tier and no signal. Rules go stale as a codebase
moves and nothing detects that automatically — regeneration is manual. And an agent
now writes to the user's global config file, which also holds provider configuration;
this is constrained to read-modify-write of its own table with an atomic rename, but
the blast radius of a bug there is larger than a sidecar's would be.

**Rejected: a repo-committed `.er/importance.toml`.** Importance is genuinely repo
knowledge that a team would want in version control, and this was the strongest
argument against the decision. It was rejected because per-repo config
(`.er-config.toml`) was removed for cause — a repo-local override permanently shadowed
global theme saves and a stale-reload path clobbered unsaved desktop settings.
Reintroducing repo-local config under a new filename reopens that failure. If team
sharing becomes a real requirement, the answer is an export/import of the table, not a
second config source.

**Rejected: showing the computed count alongside declared rules.** Attractive as a
staleness hint ("this rule says isolated, but 200 things import it"), and the right
end state — but only once the counting is accurate enough to show. Revisit after
language-aware parsing.
